Article Title: WhatsApp puts multiple accounts under review, temporarily blocks access for users
Article Text:
A WhatsApp spokesperson acknowledged that errors can occur while enforcing the platform's safety measures.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Multiple WhatsApp users including several in India reported that their accounts had been placed "under review" for 24 hours, temporarily blocking access to the messaging platform's features without prior warning.The disruption surfaced around 8pm IST on Monday, with affected users sharing screenshots showing a message from the Meta-owned app stating that their accounts were being reviewed to verify compliance with WhatsApp's terms of service. The notification read that account activity and device information were being checked and that users would typically receive a decision within 24 hours.Responding a report by PTI, a WhatsApp spokesperson acknowledged that errors can occur while enforcing the platform's safety measures."We are always working to stay ahead of those trying to abuse our service and ban accounts to help keep other users safe. Sometimes we get this wrong and if we do, we try to fix it as quickly as possible to get people back to chatting," the spokesperson said.The app also directed affected users to guidance on responsible use of WhatsApp and information relating to stolen phones and accounts.Several users took to social media to complain that their accounts had been disabled despite using the official version of the app.One user wrote: "My WhatsApp account has been disabled without any explanation. I have already submitted an appeal, but the review page only displays a generic message stating that it will 'typically be reviewed within 24 hours'. Help me urgently."Another user, identified as Saloni on X, posted: "My WhatsApp account was suddenly disabled without any warning. I only use the official app, and my work depends on WhatsApp. Please help. This was so unnecessary."The temporary account reviews come as WhatsApp remains under government scrutiny in India over its proposed username feature, which would allow users to communicate without sharing their phone numbers.The Centre recently received WhatsApp's response to a notice seeking clarification on the feature, which officials fear could increase phishing, impersonation, online fraud and so-called digital arrest scams. The government has directed the company not to roll out the feature in India until consultations are completed.WhatsApp has maintained that the feature is still under development and will be introduced gradually later this year. The company has said users will still need a phone number to create an account and that several safeguards, including protections against impersonation and limits on unsolicited contact, have been built into the feature.
Article Summary: Multiple WhatsApp users in India reported that their accounts had been placed "under review" for 24 hours. The disruption surfaced around 8pm IST on Monday, with affected users sharing screenshots. A WhatsApp spokesperson acknowledged that errors can occur while enforcing the platform's safety measures.

Article Title: Govt proposes mandatory Vehicle-to-Vehicle communication systems from Oct 2028 to cut road crashes
Article Text:
All new cars, passenger and goods vehicles would need to have Vehicle-to-Vehicle communication system. (PTI)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: From Oct 2028, all new two- and three-wheelers, cars, passenger and goods vehicles (including buses and trucks) would need to have Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V) communication system, as per a draft notification of the road transport ministry. The V2V technology is being rolled out to curb collisions and accidents.The recently published draft notification by road transport ministry proposes phased implementation of the V2V communication system and to start with all vehicles in categories L (two- and three-wheelers), M (passenger vehicles) and N (goods vehicles) manufactured from Oct 2027 would be required to comply with the newly-notified automotive standard, AIS-230, wherever they are equipped with V2V communication systems.The technology enables real-time exchange of speed, direction, position, and braking data between vehicles to prevent collisions at blind curves, intersections, or from drivers coming the wrong way without needing a cellular network. Each vehicle needs to be fitted with a device that will automatically detect approaching vehicles for preventing any crash.Unlike conventional vehicle-safety systems, which primarily depend on onboard sensors and driver reaction, V2V communication can provide information beyond the direct line of sight.“It is therefore expected to complement Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) and support proactive accident prevention, connected mobility and future intelligent transport applications,” the ministry said.In this case, every vehicle fitted with the V2V communication system will continuously send out their locations, speed and direction as tiny radio signals. They will also relay information on sudden braking by a vehicle ahead, forward collision risks, unsafe lane changes, wrong-way driving and the approach of emergency vehicles.The receiving vehicle’s system compares this information with its own location, speed and direction to predict a possible collision and alerts the driver for action.At a later stage, govt will also roll out the Vehicle to Infrastructure (V2I) communication system. In this case, sensors are installed with infrastructure, such as signal and power poles, edges of bridges and flyovers, and barricaded areas to alert vehicles.
Article Summary: All new cars, passenger and goods vehicles would need to have Vehicle-to-Vehicle communication system. The V2V technology is being rolled out to curb collisions and accidents. Each vehicle needs to be fitted with a device that will automatically detect approaching vehicles for preventing any crash.

Article Title: From apps to 'intent': How AI agents will rewrite the way we use next‑generation smartphones
Article Text:
The era of app icon grids on smartphones is ending soon. AI-first phones will use agents to fulfill user intents directly.

The era of scrolling through grids of colourful icons and hunting for the 'right' app is ending.

What is an AI-first phone?

AI-first smartphones promise a radically different future — one where users rarely think about apps at all.

What will it look like?

A day with an AI‑first phone

App-centric workflow: You decide to take a last-minute weekend trip. You open a search engine to find destinations, launch a travel aggregator app to search flights, hop into a hotel app to compare rooms, open a weather app to pack appropriately, and manually copy-paste reservation details into your calendar and communication apps. You tap dozens of buttons and navigate through multiple distinct user interfaces.

You decide to take a last-minute weekend trip. You open a search engine to find destinations, launch a travel aggregator app to search flights, hop into a hotel app to compare rooms, open a weather app to pack appropriately, and manually copy-paste reservation details into your calendar and communication apps. You tap dozens of buttons and navigate through multiple distinct user interfaces. The AI-first workflow: You simply say, "Find me a relaxing beach getaway for this weekend under Rs20,000 total, handle the bookings, and make sure I’m home by Sunday night for dinner."

"Flight booked on Carrier X, room reserved at Hotel Y, total cost Rs18,780. Confirm payment via Biometrics?"

This might all sound like sci-fi, but phones with such capabilities are already on the way.

What this means for platforms, business models

No downloads, no updates: Users won't install a parking app, they will ask an AI agent to pay for parking, and it will fetch the operator's terms and then complete the payment.

Users won't install a parking app, they will ask an AI agent to pay for parking, and it will fetch the operator's terms and then complete the payment. One interface, many back‑ends: The conversational layer replaces hundreds of bespoke interfaces. The value shifts from designing a tap‑heavy UI to ensuring your service is reliably callable by AI agents, which means having a robust Application Programming Interface (API), a set of rules that lets different softwares talk to each other.

The conversational layer replaces hundreds of bespoke interfaces. The value shifts from designing a tap‑heavy UI to ensuring your service is reliably callable by AI agents, which means having a robust Application Programming Interface (API), a set of rules that lets different softwares talk to each other. Discovery moves from stores to agents: Instead of optimising for store rankings, companies will optimise for being the agent's trusted choice — based on price, reliability, speed, and policy compliance.

App stores as service registries: Stores may evolve into curated directories of agent‑callable services (APIs) with verified security, privacy, and compliance badges — less about installs, more about trust.

Stores may evolve into curated directories of agent‑callable services (APIs) with verified security, privacy, and compliance badges — less about installs, more about trust. Monetisation shifts: Revenue models may tilt toward per‑action fees, subscriptions, and revenue share on agent‑completed transactions rather than one‑time downloads or ad‑heavy freemium apps.

Revenue models may tilt toward per‑action fees, subscriptions, and revenue share on agent‑completed transactions rather than one‑time downloads or ad‑heavy freemium apps. Developer pivot: Teams will build "agent skills" and robust APIs, not just UIs. The competitive edge becomes reliability, speed, and transparent pricing that AI agents can compare.

The end of the app as we know it?

For nearly two decades, our relationship with mobile technology has been governed by a single, undisputed design: the app icon grid.Ever since Apple launched the App Store in 2008, the burden of digital logistics has rested firmly on the user.Need a taxi? Open an app. Want to order dinner? Open another app. Pay a bill? Another app. Book a flight, check the news, edit a photo, send money, check your fitness, reserve a hotel, translate a menu, buy groceries — there is an app for everything.The modern smartphone is essentially a container filled with hundreds of miniature software silos, each demanding its own login, interface, permissions, subscriptions and updates.App Store and Google Play became the gateways to this digital universe, spawning a multi-billion-dollar economy that transformed companies like Apple and Google into the world's most powerful software gatekeepers.This model is about to collapse.The era of scrolling through grids of colourful icons and hunting for the 'right' app is ending.We are on the precipice of the biggest shift in consumer technology since the multi-touch screen: the rise of the 'AI-first' smartphone.Today's smartphones are built around apps because software was designed for humans to navigate manually. Every service has its own interface. Every company competes for a permanent place on the home screen. Success is measured by daily active users opening an app multiple times a day.AI-first smartphones promise a radically different future — one where users rarely think about apps at all.The devices are designed around small language models (SLMs) and multimodal AI agents that will run locally on your phone for quick, privacy‑sensitive tasks; and hand-off heavier reasoning to edge or cloud computing.The phones will discard the traditional operating system architecture of home screens, file systems, and sandboxed apps.In their place will be an 'Intent Engine' — a continuous, real-time operating layer powered by AI agents.Instead of interacting with software through apps, users will express their intent to AI agents.When a user expresses a goal — whether spoken, typed, or inferred through context — the phone's core AI agent will break down that intent into logical sub-tasks, assign actions to underlying services, and compile the result into a custom, dynamically generated view.In practice, the home screen will become a goal launcher, not an app grid.You might see tiles like 'Plan my weekend', 'What's in the news?', or 'Track expenses', each invoking an agent that orchestrates the underlying services.Without the structural necessity of cramming dozens of app icons onto a home screen, phone hardware can evolve beyond the glass slab.While touchscreens will remain vital for rich visual consumption, hardware design will prioritise contextual inputs: micro-cameras, directional arrays, health sensors, and ambient displays. The primary interface becomes voice, gesture, and subtle visual cues.Because the device is powered by an overarching agent rather than hundreds of disparate software platforms, phone performance will be pristine. Storage constraints shift from managing gigabytes of cached app binaries to hosting optimised, localised neural networks.Consider a typical scenario on a contemporary device versus an AI-first phone:The phone’s AI agent does not "open" an app. It queries hundreds of services simultaneously.It evaluates airline availability, checks boutique hotel inventory, verifies your personal calendar for conflicts, pulls your saved dietary preferences for in-flight meals, and presents a single, unified execution card:With one tap or voice confirmation, the entire transaction settles.You never browsed an app, never logged into a third-party interface, and never manually transferred a single byte of data.When you arrive at the airport the agent surfaces your boarding pass and gate changes without you opening an airline or travel app or email.When you land, the AI agent has already arranged a rental car for your transport.When you need to pay a parking fee, it identifies the lot operator, fetches terms, and pays via biometric authentication — no apps required.Over time, the phone learns your preferences and constraints, making these interactions faster and more anticipatory.Health apps would stop being destinations and become background services.Instead of jumping between sleep, fitness, medication, diet, and doctor apps, you could simply say, “Help me recover from a bad week of sleep” or “Book the earliest endocrinologist in my network,” and the phone would pull data from wearables, records, pharmacies, labs, and calendars to act on your behalf.That would make health management far more proactive. The phone could spot problems early — a rising resting heart rate, missed medication, or a sleep pattern going off track — and respond before you even open an app.The same shift would hit financial apps even harder.Rather than using separate banking, payments, budgeting, tax, and bill-pay apps, you could say, “Pay my credit card, move the rest to savings, and warn me if travel spending goes over budget,” and the phone would handle it in the background.This might all sound like sci-fi, but phones with such capabilities are already in the advanced production stage and the underlying technology has already been proven. As AI automates more of our routine digital interactions, the focus will shift from managing apps to engaging with curated experiences, from structured wellness journeys to step-by-step lessons in finance and investing The app store model has been the single most lucrative cash cow in modern technology history.Platforms like Apple and Google extract up to a 30% commission on digital purchases, while controlling distribution, user acquisition, and developer access.The rise of agentic AI threatens to disassemble this walled-garden economy entirely.Market research firm Gartner last year projected that mobile app usage will drop 25% by 2027 as AI assistants absorb routine tasks, a trend already visible in how people use AI tools instead of opening multiple apps for research, drafting, and scheduling.App stores were built for a world where software arrived as siloed products with their own user interfaces (UI) and update cycles.AI agents invert that model:The app economy won't vanish overnight, but its centre of gravity will move:Brands will no longer compete on who has the slickest app design or the most addicting engagement loops; they will compete on execution speed, data reliability, and service quality.A food delivery service won't win customers by optimising 'dark patterns' in its app; it will win because its backend API offers the fastest delivery times and lowest rates when an AI agent compares options on behalf of a user.Businesses won't simply ask:"How do we rank first on Google?"They'll ask:"How do we become our customer's AI's preferred choice?"Predictions about the death of apps should be treated cautiously. Email survived instant messaging. Websites survived social media. Desktop software survived cloud computing.Apps are unlikely to vanish completely.Many professional tools, creative applications, games and specialised software will still benefit from rich, dedicated user interfaces. A graphic designer editing a complex image or a gamer playing a visually intensive title will continue to rely on purpose-built applications.But for the vast majority of everyday smartphone interactions, the trend points in a different direction.Booking travel, paying bills, getting news updates, shopping, scheduling appointments, managing subscriptions and countless other routine tasks are increasingly suited to conversational AI that can coordinate multiple services behind the scenes.Just as few people think about the networking protocols that power the internet, future users may stop thinking about apps altogether. They will simply tell their phones what they want, and the AI will decide how to make it happen.If the smartphone era was defined by tapping icons, the next chapter may be defined by something far simpler: asking.And when software becomes something you ask rather than something you open, the app store no longer sits at the center of the mobile experience. It becomes the plumbing behind it.For users, the payoff is simplicity: fewer icons, fewer logins, fewer steps.For builders, the mandate is clear: design for agents — reliable APIs, transparent pricing, and policies that make your service the obvious trustable choice when the phone decides on the user's behalf.
Article Summary: The era of app icon grids on smartphones is ending soon. AI-first phones will use agents to fulfill user intents directly. The value shifts from designing a tap‑heavy UI to ensuring your service is reliably callable by AI agents.

Article Title: Scientists have built robot that has one practical mission: Keeping tabs on great white shark to protect swimmers
Article Text:
Representative Image of a futuristic robot

Shark-spotting robots said to monitor a beach for up to a week

Drone to provide an aerial view of the water

Scientists in California are reportedly developing a semi-autonomous robot designed to detect great white sharks near beaches and give researchers and lifeguards more information about their movements. According to a report by the New York Post, researchers at California State University, Long Beach’s Shark Lab have unveiled the Shark Surveillance Bot (SSB), which can patrol waters just offshore. Once fully operational, the robot will “listen” for great white sharks fitted with tracking tags. At the same time, it will collect water samples to search for shark environmental DNA, or eDNA — genetic traces that sharks leave in the water through skin cells, blood and other biological material.The project is being developed by the Shark Lab in collaboration with New York University’s Center of Robotics and the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute. It is funded by the Seaver Institute. The robots, the lab said will “be capable of patrolling off a beach, listening for tagged white sharks, sampling water for shark eDNA, and will have a drone nest on the back for aerial surveillance”.As stated in the report, researchers hope the Shark Surveillance Bot will eventually be able to remain near an individual beach for as long as a week, continuously gathering information about sharks in the area.The aim is not simply to detect whether a shark is nearby. Scientists want to better understand which sharks are present and how many are moving around popular beaches.“Our data suggests that there are sharks around our beaches all the time without incident,” Shark Lab Director Christopher Lowe told KTLA as quoted in the report. “Knowing what sharks, and how many are out there helps lifeguards make better decisions in beach safety operations and in advising the public.”The robot will detect signals from great white sharks that researchers have previously fitted with tracking tags. Its water-sampling system will provide another way of looking for evidence of sharks through environmental DNA.The shark-monitoring robot will also work with an aerial drone. The drone will sit on the robot and can be launched to provide researchers with a bird’s-eye view of the surrounding ocean. The system will combine this aerial footage with 360-degree video and shark-tracking data. Information can then be sent back to the Shark Lab over Wi-Fi.Researchers hope the technology could eventually provide lifeguards with near real-time information about shark activity, helping them make beach safety decisions based on more detailed data.
Article Summary: Shark-spotting robots said to monitor a beach for up to a week. Drone to provide an aerial view of the water for more detailed data. Technology could eventually provide lifeguards with near real-time information about shark activity, helping them make beach safety decisions.

Article Title: Uber CTO Praveen Neppalli Naga who sparked Tokenmaxxing panic has another lesson on using AI
Article Text:
Uber CTO says productivity boost comes from workflow redesign



Uber CTO says company is moving beyond ‘Tokenmaxxing’



Earlier this year, Uber’s CTO Praveen Neppalli Naga triggered a “tokenmaxxing panic” after revealing the company nearly blew through its 2026 budget for Anthropic’s Claude Code in just three months. Now, Naga is back with a new lesson. According to a report by Business Insider, Naga said that the biggest gains from AI don’t come from speeding up single tasks, but from redesigning the complete workflows. Naga said that Uber has started deploying its best AI engineers into departments like finance, legal, marketing, HR and procurement. These two-week teams, dubbed Agentic Pods, shadow employees for several days to understand workflows, then rapidly build and test AI-powered tools.The results have been dramatic:* Financial planning cut from 15 hours to 30 minutes.* Financial reports reduced from two days to 10 minutes.* Marketing quality checks shrank from two weeks to under an hour.Naga emphasised that the real productivity boost comes from workflow redesign — eliminating redundant approvals, replacing outdated software, and enabling faster decision-making. Several executives compared the approach to Silicon Valley’s forward-deployed engineer model, but with a twist: instead of embedding engineers with customers, Uber is embedding them inside its own operations.Vantortech CPO Peter Wilczynski jokingly dubbed the role the “Rearward Deployed Engineer”, describing specialists embedded deep inside corporate processes to reimagine how work gets done with AI.To bridge the gap between high AI costs and real-world efficiency, Uber launched a project called “Agentic Pods”. The goal was to stop treating AI as an expensive experiment and start using it to redesign complex, manual workflows across departments like Finance, Legal and Marketing.Naga said that the company handpicked approximately 30 of its most AI-proficient engineers and paired them directly with domain experts – the employees who actually perform the work. The teams operated on a strict, two-week schedule. The claimed that in just two months, Uber successfully ran 16 of these “Agentic Pods” across 16 different business functions, and noted that the efficiency gains were significant.
Article Summary: Uber CTO Praveen Neppalli Naga says company is moving beyond ‘Tokenmaxxing’ Naga said that the biggest gains from AI don’t come from speeding up single tasks, but from redesigning the complete workflows.

Article Title: Jamie Dimon: We are very protective of our data, you should assume that JPMorgan will do everything it can
Article Text:
Jamie Dimon said ‘We are very protective of our data and IP’



Rise of ‘modelmaxxing’



Jamie Dimon responds to him taking up 'White House job



Jamie Dimon, CEO of America’s biggest bank says that the era of unchecked AI spending is over, warning that businesses must treat AI ‘like any other resource’ as costs rise sharply. According to a report by Business Insider, speaking in an interview on CNBC, Dimon said that the companies are becoming more disciplined about token spend which is the usage-based cost of running AI models and increasingly focused on return on investment. He also noted that the companies are already shifting queries to cheaper tokens, and that similar cost-squeezing will happen across power and data-centre usage as AI adoption expands.Dimon also noted a growing concern among executives: data security in the age of generative AI. “We are very protective of our data and our IP,” he said. “You should assume that JPMorgan will do everything they can to protect its own data, its own IP, to protect our customers.” His comments reflect a broader shift among large enterprises, many of which are tightening controls around proprietary information as AI vendors seek more access to customer data to improve model performance.Dimon’s remarks place him among a growing group of business leaders advocating modelmaxxing — choosing the right‑sized, cost‑efficient AI model rather than defaulting to the most powerful (and expensive) frontier systems. This trend is a direct response to tokenmaxxing, where companies overuse high‑cost AI tools like Claude, Codex and Cursor in ways that add little value.Palantir CEO Alex Karp has been one of the strongest critics of tokenmaxxing, saying AI models have been “oversold” and that many companies are wasting money on tokens that deliver no meaningful returns. He even compared compulsive AI usage to porn addiction, calling it "demastinatory" behavior inside enterprises. Cerebras Systems CEO Andrew Feldman echoed the sentiment, saying unlimited token budgets were “boneheaded from the get‑go. ” His analogy: “You don’t need a Ferrari to go to the grocery store… use a lower‑cost open‑source model.”In related news, Jamie Dimon recently offered some fresh insight into what he might do once he eventually steps down from his position. Dimon said that he is more likely to write a book or teach than pursue politics. Speaking to Axios in an interview, Dimon said that he would focus on doing business ‘with people I like’ and possibly explore media-related projects. Dimon also addressed the speculation that he could be headed for the White House, saying there is “pretty much no chance” he would run for office. “I’m very hard-pressed to think I should be doing something like that,” he said with a laugh, adding that he’s never been part of a campaign. The JPMorgan CEO cited his age (70) and past health issues including emergency heart surgery in 2020 and throat cancer in 2014, as reasons politics is unlikely.
Article Summary: Jamie Dimon, CEO of America’s biggest bank says that the era of unchecked AI spending is over. Warns that businesses must treat AI ‘like any other resource’ as costs rise sharply. Dimon also addressed the speculation that he could be headed for the White House, saying there is ‘pretty much no chance’ he would run for office.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works







Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness.

Article Title: Quote of the day by JS Mill: 'I have learned to seek my happiness by limiting my desires, rather than...' and the 19th-century cure for modern burnout
Article Text:
John Stuart Mill was a 19th-century philosopher who argued that true happiness comes from developing the mind

I have learned to seek my happiness by limiting my desires, rather than in attempting to satisfy them.”

The breakdown of a calculating mind

The utilitarian paradox

Curbing the engine of infinite wants

A shopper standing in the middle of a brightly lit superstore, holding three slightly different versions of the same household item, often feels an odd sense of confusion rather than freedom. The endless scroll of online stores promises that the perfect product to complete life is just one click away. Yet, as packages keep arriving at the door, the promised happiness often disappears, replaced by a lingering desire for whatever comes next.This cycle of endless consumption is exactly what the Victorian philosopher John Stuart Mill described when he wrote: “Mill’s observation completely changes the usual idea of finding happiness. Instead of seeing human desire as an endless list of needs that must be fulfilled, he argued that desire itself is what needs to be controlled. Satisfaction, in his view, does not come from building a bigger net to catch every passing impulse, but from reducing what we expect and demand from the world.John Stuart Mill published this reflection in his Autobiography in 1873, a book describing one of the most intense intellectual upbringings in Western history.Born in London in 1806, Mill was raised under a strict educational experiment designed by his father, James Mill, and the founder of Utilitarianism, Jeremy Bentham. By the age of three, he was learning Ancient Greek; by eight, he was reading Herodotus and Plato in their original language; and by his early teens, he had mastered political economy and formal logic.The purpose of this education was to create a perfectly rational follower of Bentham—a person trained to judge every action by calculating how to produce the greatest pleasure and the least pain for the greatest number of people.The experiment seemed successful until 1826, when twenty-year-old Mill suffered a serious mental breakdown. In one of the most famous parts of his memoir, Mill recalled asking himself a simple question: if all his political and social goals were achieved tomorrow, would he truly feel happy? His honest answer was an immediate “no.” His highly rational way of thinking had left him emotionally empty.Mill’s recovery happened gradually, helped by the poetry of William Wordsworth and by a major reconsideration of Utilitarian philosophy. He realized that Bentham’s basic idea—treating happiness as simply the total of fulfilled desires—was deeply incomplete. To recover his peace of mind, Mill had to rethink what true well-being meant. The quotation from his Autobiography marks this important turning point, showing his realization that lasting happiness comes from controlling desire rather than satisfying every new craving.To understand Mill’s change in thinking, we must examine a tension within Utilitarian philosophy. Traditional Utilitarianism viewed happiness as the total amount of pleasure minus pain. If people could continue creating and satisfying new desires, happiness should, in theory, continue increasing.Mill recognized the major problem with this idea: human desires constantly grow. As soon as one desire is fulfilled, our expectations rise again, a pattern that modern psychologists call the “hedonic treadmill.” Trying to find lasting happiness by satisfying every new want is like trying to fill a bucket full of holes.By encouraging people to limit their desires, Mill was not promoting extreme self-denial or the lifestyle of monks. Instead, he brought his updated version of Utilitarianism closer to older philosophical traditions. Epicurus had argued centuries earlier that simple, easily achieved pleasures bring the greatest peace of mind, while Stoic thinkers such as Seneca believed that true wealth comes not from owning many things, but from wanting fewer things.Mill adapted this idea for the modern industrial world. He argued that higher intellectual and emotional pleasures—such as art, friendship, public service, and personal development—are naturally more valuable than endlessly collecting material possessions. Limiting material and superficial desires frees mental energy, allowing people to develop deeper, non-material sources of happiness that do not lose their value once they are achieved.In 2026, Mill’s insight speaks directly to one of the biggest challenges of modern life: the commercialization of human attention and desire. Today’s digital systems are carefully designed to constantly create new wants that can only be satisfied through more consumption. Targeted algorithms, personalized advertising, and micro-influencers work together to convince people that something important is always missing from their lives.The growing popularity of voluntary simplicity, digital minimalism, and anti-consumption movements reflects Mill’s principle in action. When technology workers switch to basic feature phones or consumers commit to “no-buy” years, they are putting his idea into practice. They are not doing so because they lack money, but because they want to break the endless cycle of constantly creating new desires.The same principle also applies to work and professional burnout. Modern workplaces often define success through constant growth: higher salaries, bigger teams, and continuous promotions. However, research in behavioral economics consistently shows that once people reach a comfortable middle-class standard of living, extra income brings smaller and smaller increases in everyday happiness. Executives who reject promotions to protect their personal lives or professionals who choose lower-paying jobs for better health are deciding to reduce their ambitions rather than spend their lives chasing ever-growing demands.By describing happiness as the relationship between what people have and what they want, Mill offered a lasting mathematical insight: the result can be improved either by increasing what you have or by reducing what you want.When Mill died in Avignon in 1873, he left behind writings that influenced modern liberal democracy, individual freedom, and economic thought. Yet perhaps his greatest personal achievement was overcoming the crisis of his youth. By understanding that peace of mind depends on controlling desire instead of constantly feeding it, he left a timeless guide for staying mentally balanced in a world designed to keep people forever wanting more.
Article Summary: John Stuart Mill was a 19th-century philosopher who argued that true happiness comes from developing the mind. He argued that desire itself is what needs to be controlled. Limiting material and superficial desires frees mental energy, allowing people to develop deeper, non-material sources of happiness.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Bertrand Russell: 'There are two motives for reading a book; one, that you enjoy it; the other...' and how most of us are guilty of the second
Article Text:
Bertrand Russell was a British philosopher, logician, mathematician, and one of the most influential thinkers of the 20th century.

"There are two motives for reading a book; one, that you enjoy it; the other, that you can boast about it,"

A philosopher’s critique of modern anxiety

The psychology of social performance

Performative reading in the digital age

Finding the private joy in pages

Walk into a crowded coffee shop or scroll through social media, and you will quickly spot a familiar ritual. A heavy paperbound volume of James Joyce’s Ulysses or David Foster Wallace’s Infinite Jest lies open on a small wooden table. Its owner glances around, sips an espresso, and leaves the spine clearly visible to passersby.wrote British philosopher Bertrand Russell in his 1930 book The Conquest of Happiness.Russell captured a quiet truth about human behaviour. Reading serves two completely different masters: private satisfaction and public status. While we like to imagine that every turned page stems from pure curiosity, our desire for intellectual prestige often drives us to pick up books we have no real intention of finishing.Russell wrote The Conquest of Happiness during a period of massive social change in post-World War I Britain. As literacy rates climbed and mass-market publishing expanded across Europe, books became accessible consumer goods rather than rare luxuries.In a chapter titled Byronic Unhappiness, Russell analyzed how modern urban life encouraged superficial intellectualism. People bought dense philosophical treatises and classic literature not to absorb their ideas, but to signal membership in an educated upper class.Russell’s target was not reading itself. As a logician who co-wrote the three-volume mathematical landmark Principia Mathematica with Alfred North Whitehead, he valued rigorous study. Instead, he targeted the widespread anxiety caused by doing things purely for social approval. He argued that reading out of obligation or vanity turned a potentially joyful habit into exhausting performance art.Russell’s distinction connects directly to simple psychological ideas about human motivation.In the 1970s, psychologists Edward L. Deci and Richard M. Ryan developed Self-Determination Theory. This idea separates two types of motivation: intrinsic motivation (doing an activity simply because you enjoy it) and extrinsic motivation (doing something to gain outside rewards, attention, or status). Reading for personal fun is a classic intrinsic activity. Reading to build an impressive public reputation relies entirely on extrinsic social approval.Sociologist Pierre Bourdieu explored this same tension in his 1979 book Distinction: A Social Critique of the Judgement of Taste. Bourdieu showed how educated groups use cultural knowledge, including familiar books, classical music, and fine art, to mark subtle boundaries between social classes. Displaying a thick, challenging book serves as a silent signal of leisure time, education, and high standing.When people buy books primarily to brag about them, they fall into what social psychologist Erich Fromm called the "having mode" of existence. Instead of entering the "being mode," which means engaging deeply with an author's ideas and allowing those ideas to shape their worldview, they treat books as physical trophies to collect and show off.Russell's observation hits harder today than when he published it nearly a century ago. Digital platforms have turned reading into a tracked, public performance sport.On social media platforms like Goodreads, users publicly display annual reading goals, logging 50 or 100 books a year in a race against arbitrary numbers. On Instagram and TikTok, short video creators build personal channels around carefully arranged bookshelf tours, color-coordinated book displays, and monthly reading wrap-up videos. The term "tsundoku," which is a Japanese word for buying books and letting them pile up unread, has become a popular badge of honor online.This performative culture creates measurable changes in reading habits. Pierre Bayard, a literature professor at the University of Paris VIII, published an honest study in 2007 titled How to Talk About Books You Haven't Read. Bayard noted that in academic and social circles, people routinely pretend to have read major classics to protect their social standing and avoid looking uneducated.When readers choose books based on what looks impressive on a digital profile, they often abandon books that offer genuine personal delight. Easy fiction, light mysteries, and graphic novels get pushed aside in favor of lengthy biographies or dense histories that sit half-read on bedside tables.When reading becomes a public performance, it loses its power to rest the mind. Trying to read books you dislike just to impress strangers turns a peaceful hobby into another source of daily stress.Russell believed that true happiness requires direct, unforced engagement with the world. Reading for genuine pleasure allows a person to lose track of time, enter new ideas, and learn without keeping score. It provides a rare quiet space where you do not need to prove anything to anyone.A room full of unread books is not a personal failure, provided those books were chosen with real curiosity rather than vanity. The true value of a personal library lies not in how impressive it looks to visitors, but in how deeply its contents belong to the reader sitting quietly in the chair.
Article Summary: Bertrand Russell wrote The Conquest of Happiness during a period of massive social change in post-World War I Britain. He argued that reading out of obligation or vanity turned a potentially joyful habit into exhausting performance art. Digital platforms have turned reading into a tracked, public performance sport. Reading for genuine pleasure allows a person to lose track of time and learn new ideas.

Article Title: In the early 1900s, the USDA distributed torpedograss as cattle feed; its torpedo-shaped roots later invaded southern wetlands and waterways
Article Text:
Torpedograss, introduced for livestock forage, now invades southern United States wetlands. This grass spreads efficiently through underground rhizomes, making it difficult to control. It forms dense stands, outcompeting native vegetation and altering plant communities. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons

How torpedograss spread beyond pastureland

Management efforts often require repeated applications of herbicides and mechanical removal. Preventing rhizome fragment movement is crucial to limit further spread. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons

Why it has become difficult to manage

A grass that was once promoted for agricultural use has since become a persistent invasive plant across parts of the southern United States. Today, torpedograss is found in wetlands, marshes, canals, lakes and riverbanks, where it spreads rapidly, competes with native vegetation and becomes difficult to manage once established.The US Fish and Wildlife Service's Ecological Risk Screening Summary for Torpedograss explains how the species expanded within the United States after the US Department of Agriculture distributed it more widely during the early 1900s for use as livestock forage. According to the assessment, the species has biological traits that allow it to spread efficiently, survive under different environmental conditions and form dense stands once established. These characteristics have contributed to its continued spread across suitable habitats in the southern United States.Although torpedograss was introduced because of its value as forage, the same qualities that made it attractive for agriculture later allowed it to spread into waterways and wetlands. The assessment describes the species as a high ecological risk because it can establish, persist and spread in suitable environments.Torpedograss, or Panicum repens, is native to parts of Africa, Europe and Asia.As per the US Fish and Wildlife Service's Ecological Risk Screening Summary, the species had already been introduced into the United States before 1876. The assessment notes that the US Department of Agriculture later distributed the grass more widely during the early twentieth century for forage, allowing it to become established across additional parts of the southern United States.One defining feature is its torpedo-shaped underground rhizomes, which give torpedograss its common name. Instead of depending mainly on seeds, the grass spreads through these underground stems. Even small rhizome fragments left in the soil can produce new plants, making the species difficult to remove once it has become established.The report explains that these underground stems also help the grass spread when soil, water or machinery moves rhizome fragments from one location to another. Floodwaters and routine land management activities can unintentionally transport these pieces into new areas, where they are capable of growing into fresh colonies.Another reason for its continued expansion is its ability to grow under a variety of environmental conditions. The assessment notes that torpedograss can establish in both wet and relatively dry habitats. As a result, it can grow along the edges of lakes, ponds, marshes, canals and drainage systems, as well as in some agricultural landscapes.Because of these characteristics, the species has become established across much of the southeastern United States, particularly in warm regions where climatic conditions support its growth.According to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service assessment, torpedograss often forms thick stands that can replace existing vegetation. As these dense patches expand, they can crowd out native plant species. Dense growth may also interfere with the normal use of waterways, including navigation and water management in some locations.Torpedograss also grows outside natural habitats, including agricultural areas, where its ability to spread through underground rhizomes can make control more challenging. Simply removing the visible shoots is often not enough because rhizomes remaining beneath the soil surface can produce new growth.The US Fish and Wildlife Service assessment indicates that established infestations can be difficult to control because rhizomes remaining beneath the soil surface are capable of producing new shoots, meaning repeated management efforts may be needed. The assessment discusses a combination of approaches, including herbicide application and mechanical control, while noting that complete removal can be difficult once large infestations have developed.According to the US Fish and Wildlife Service assessment, limiting the movement of rhizome fragments into unaffected areas is important because they can be carried in contaminated soil, water or equipment and establish new infestations. Cleaning equipment, limiting the transport of contaminated soil and identifying new infestations early can help reduce further spread before the grass becomes firmly established.Torpedograss illustrates how an introduced forage plant can become a long-term environmental problem after escaping cultivation.
Article Summary: Torpedograss, introduced for livestock forage, now invades southern United States wetlands. This grass spreads efficiently through underground rhizomes, making it difficult to control. It forms dense stands, outcompeting native vegetation and altering plant communities. Management efforts often require repeated applications of herbicides and mechanical removal.

How Jacob Tsimerman became a Fields Medal-winning mathematician



Why did he decide to join OpenAI?

He believes AI could transform mathematics itself



Looking beyond academia

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.

Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.

This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

Article Title: Before the knowledge walks out the door
Article Text:
Everyone in Silicon Valley is racing to build machines that replace human expertise.

Ahmer Inam

, a schoolteacher's son from Delhi, is building machines that inherit it.

When Ahmer Inam appeared on Fox & Friends in June, his mother watched the segment without following much of it. Her English is limited. There was her son on the famous curved couch of American morning television, fielding questions about artificial intelligence, and she understood almost none of the words. She wept anyway. Some distances need no translation, and the one between a schoolteacher's household in Delhi and a Manhattan television studio is legible in any language.Had she followed the argument, it might have surprised her less than it surprised the audience. Because what Inam was defending, underneath the vocabulary of frontier AI, is approximately the oldest idea in civilisation — the one his father practised for a living: that knowledge survives only when one generation troubles to hand it to the next.Inam has spent twenty-five years building artificial intelligence — long enough to remember when it meant symbolic logic in the late nineties, and senior enough to have run AI and data for Fortune 500 companies, Nike and Wells Fargo among them, back when "chief AI officer" was still an exotic title. He is not, in other words, a critic sniping from the cheap seats. Which makes the thesis of Cognisee, the research lab he founded and leads, sound almost seditious in today's Silicon Valley: "We're not trying to replace the worker," he says."We're trying to make the worker irreplaceable."The problem he is aiming at usually gets filed under the bland heading of "labour shortage." By one estimate, more than two million skilled-trade jobs in the United States could sit unfilled by 2030 — electricians, welders, machinists, the hands America needs if it is serious about building factories, chip plants and grid capacity again. But Inam's diagnosis is sharper than a headcount. "America does not have a work shortage," he likes to say. "It has an expertise shortage."Consider what actually leaves the building when a master electrician retires at sixty-eight. Not the manual — the manual stays. What leaves is the ear that catches a motor running slightly wrong two weeks before it fails; the instinct that connects a faint vibration to a pattern in old maintenance logs; forty years of judgment that was never written down because it could not be. The philosopher Michael Polanyi had a name for this — tacit knowledge, the things we know but cannot tell — and Cognisee is, at bottom, a bet that the most valuable training data on earth is tacit.The company's method has a fable-like symmetry. Its AI begins as an apprentice: it works alongside experienced people and learns what they notice, what they ask, how they make judgment calls. Then it turns around and becomes a coach, carrying that accumulated judgment to the newcomer. "First it's an apprentice," Inam says. "Then it becomes a coach." Picture a 22-year-old on his first aircraft-maintenance job, hearing a sound he has never heard before, with the distilled instincts of the country's best technicians beside him in real time. "He's not being replaced by a machine," Inam says. "He's being mentored by one."The repository where all this lives is called, a little grandly, a Wisdom Vault — a secure library of hard-won know-how from doctors, nurses, electricians, factory workers, farmers, small-business owners. Grand or not, the name gives away the emotional register Inam is working in. This is not pitched as workforce optimisation. It is pitched as inheritance.He is careful — insistent, actually — about the question that framing invites: who owns it? In Cognisee's design, the expert decides what to preserve, what to share, and with whom; the contributor is recognised and rewarded; the knowledge belongs to the person who earned it, not to the machine that absorbed it. "There is a big difference," Inam says, "between being monitored and being mentored." The company is incorporated as a public benefit corporation, which he describes as a legal commitment to the worker rather than a marketing pledge.That ownership principle is also where his quarrel with the reigning AI paradigm becomes explicit. The frontier labs, Inam argues, got intelligent by swallowing the written internet — and the written internet is now substantially swallowed, which is why the industry's plan increasingly amounts to bigger data centres and more electricity, even as some of the field's own pioneers warn of a wall ahead. His contrarian wager is that the next leap will come not from more compute but from the knowledge that never made it onto the internet in the first place — and that it can be gathered by consent rather than by crawler.For an Indian reader, the resonance is hard to miss. This is a country that has watched its weaves, its remedies and its craft knowledge catalogued, carried off and sold back to it before. It is also a country whose deepest teaching traditions were never textual at all, but moved from person to person — the guru-shishya parampara, the ustad and the shagird. Inam has spoken about Wisdom Vaults for indigenous and medicinal knowledge, with communities retaining ownership of what they contribute. One way to describe Cognisee is as an attempt to give the world's oral inheritances an infrastructure layer — sovereignty included.The idea is attracting converts from unexpected quarters. Cognisee's co-founder, Alex Giannou, spent nearly two decades on Wall Street financing precisely the data centres and power deals behind the AI boom; he crossed over, in Inam's telling, because the right bet and the smart bet turned out to be the same one. Among the company's early backers is a senior Google executive who helped invent federated learning, one of the foundational privacy-preserving techniques of modern machine learning. And last year the XPRIZE Foundation, where Inam serves as a Visionary, recognised his work with its Global Visioneering Award.None of which quite explains the conviction. For that you have to go back to Delhi. Inam grew up in a low-income household, the son of a teacher — a man who spent his working life on the least scalable expertise-transfer technology ever devised: one adult, one room, one generation at a time. The son's journey to America was not gilded; there were stretches, early on, when he could not always afford to eat. It takes a particular kind of person to emerge from that and conclude that a nation's most undervalued asset sits not in its server farms but in the heads of its retiring machinists and nurses."Every generation should start where the last one left off," Inam says. It sounds like a product principle. It is closer to a family creed — the thing his father practised without ever calling it a thesis, the thing his mother recognised on a television screen in a language she does not speak. Some knowledge, it turns out, transfers just fine.
Article Summary: Ahmer Inam, a schoolteacher's son from Delhi, is building machines that inherit it. The problem he is aiming at usually gets filed under the bland heading of "labour shortage" By one estimate, more than two million skilled-trade jobs in the United States could sit unfilled by 2030.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Jensen Huang: "If you want to do something new, you have to be willing to fail."
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Jensen Huang: What does it mean?

Why did Jensen Huang say this?

How failure helped build Nvidia





Why failure is essential for innovation

Lessons everyone can learn from this quote

Why the quote is relevant in today's AI era







A timeless lesson on courage and innovation

Innovation has always demanded courage, and few technology leaders embody that principle better than Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang. As the driving force behind one of the world's most valuable technology companies, Huang has spent decades pushing the boundaries of graphics computing and artificial intelligence. Along the way, he has experienced setbacks, uncertainty and difficult decisions that ultimately shaped Nvidia's success. His quote, "If you want to do something new, you have to be willing to fail," captures the reality that every meaningful breakthrough begins with risk. Rather than fearing failure, Huang encourages people to embrace it as an essential step towards learning, innovation and long-term success.Jensen Huang's quote highlights a fundamental truth about innovation: doing something truly original always involves uncertainty. Whether someone is launching a business, developing a new technology or learning a new skill, there is no guarantee of immediate success. New ideas often require experimentation, and experiments do not always work the first time.Instead of treating failure as a setback, Huang believes it should be viewed as a valuable learning experience.Every mistake teaches lessons that can improve future decisions and bring people closer to success. His message encourages individuals to stop fearing failure and start seeing it as an unavoidable part of growth.Huang has shared this philosophy in several public discussions about entrepreneurship and innovation. Throughout Nvidia's history, he has explained that companies attempting revolutionary ideas cannot expect every decision to succeed. The willingness to take calculated risks has been central to Nvidia's journey since it was founded in 1993.During its early years, Nvidia faced fierce competition and significant financial pressure. Several products failed to meet expectations, and the company came close to running out of money. Rather than abandoning its vision, Huang and his team continued refining their technology until they found success in graphics processing units, which later became the foundation of the artificial intelligence boom.Today, Nvidia is recognised as one of the world's leading AI companies, but its success was built over decades of persistence rather than overnight achievements. Many of the company's innovations were the result of repeated experimentation and continuous improvement.Its graphics processing units, originally developed for video games, eventually became essential tools for artificial intelligence, scientific computing, robotics and autonomous vehicles. Huang has often pointed to this transformation as proof that embracing uncertainty and learning from setbacks can create opportunities that were impossible to predict at the beginning.History shows that some of humanity's greatest discoveries emerged only after repeated failures. Inventors, scientists and entrepreneurs frequently spend years testing ideas before finding one that works. Every unsuccessful attempt eliminates one possibility and brings them closer to the right solution.Huang believes innovation cannot exist without this process. People who refuse to risk failure often choose familiar paths, while those willing to experiment are more likely to discover something genuinely new. In fast-moving industries such as artificial intelligence, the ability to learn quickly from mistakes has become a major competitive advantage.The message extends well beyond the technology sector. Students preparing for examinations, professionals changing careers and entrepreneurs starting new ventures all face uncertainty. Success rarely comes without obstacles, and setbacks often provide the experience needed for future achievements.Rather than becoming discouraged by failure, Huang encourages people to remain curious, adaptable and resilient. A rejected job application, an unsuccessful project or a failed business idea does not define a person's future. What matters is the willingness to learn, improve and try again.Artificial intelligence is transforming industries across the world, creating both opportunities and challenges. As organisations race to develop new AI tools and applications, experimentation has become more important than ever. Many research projects fail before producing a breakthrough, but those failures often generate valuable knowledge.Huang's advice is particularly relevant because AI development depends on continuous testing and improvement. His words remind innovators that meaningful progress requires patience, resilience and a willingness to accept temporary setbacks in pursuit of long-term goals.Jensen Huang's quote is more than just advice for entrepreneurs. It is a reminder that every remarkable achievement begins with the courage to try something unfamiliar. Fear of failure can prevent people from reaching their full potential, while the willingness to accept mistakes often leads to unexpected opportunities.As technology continues to reshape the world, Huang's message remains timeless. Those who dare to innovate, learn from failure and keep moving forward are often the ones who create the ideas that change industries and improve lives
Article Summary: "If you want to do something new, you have to be willing to fail" is the quote of the day by Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang. Huang has spent decades pushing the boundaries of graphics computing and artificial intelligence. He believes that every meaningful breakthrough begins with risk.

Article Title: Andrej Karpathy’s ‘Lord of the Rings’ experiment shows how testing of AI models have changed and what they lack
Article Text:
Moving beyond benchmarks to on-demand worlds



Key technical limitations in visual auditing



AI researcher Andrej Karpathy, who joined Anthropic earlier this year, recently put Claude Opus 5 through a unique coding test, demonstrating how benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) are evolving past simple tasks into complex software engineering. Moving beyond standard prompts like generating basic 2D graphics or short text snippets, Karpathy gave the model the opening paragraph of J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Lord of the Rings and a $10 budget allocation of 1 million tokens. The also commanded the AI model render the scene as an interactive 3D web environment using Three.js – JavaScript library used to create and display animated 3D computer graphics in a web browser.Karpathy said in a post on X (formerly Twitter) that over the course of two hours, the AI model operated autonomously to write 5,500 lines of JavaScript code. The output produced a low-poly, procedurally generated 3D rendering of the Shire – complete with hobbit holes, trees, rivers, character assets and ambient animations synchronised with narrated book excerpts.While Karpathy noted that while the visual rendering had noticeable flaws, he pointed out that the experiment underscores a fundamental shift in how developers can test AI capabilities.Orchestrating thousands of polygon assets across complex 3D coordinate systems requires a level of computational patience that humans rarely dedicate to hyper-specific tasks.“We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all,” Karpathy said in the post.“I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand,” he added.Despite the milestone, the test also highlighted significant gaps in current frontier models. Because LLMs lack native, real-time video perception and the ability to seamlessly interact with live environments, the model struggled to audit its own visual output.“Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking,” Karpathy pointed out.
Article Summary: AI researcher Andrej Karpathy recently put Claude Opus 5 through a unique coding test. The test demonstrated how benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) are evolving past simple tasks into complex software engineering. The experiment underscores a fundamental shift in how developers can test AI capabilities.
